opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When people say "end-to-end" in autonomous driving, I think the term has become a bit of a marketing label, so first I'd separate what it means technically from what it promises.

Technically, end-to-end means you train a single model, or a tightly coupled stack, that goes from raw sensor input, mostly camera pixels, straight to driving actions or trajectories. You don't hand-design the intermediate interfaces: no explicit perception module outputting bounding boxes, no rule-based planner on top. The appeal is real. Every hand-designed interface loses information, and every hand-written rule eventually meets a corner case it didn't anticipate. Letting gradients flow through the whole system lets the model decide what matters. That's the same lesson we've seen in language, in vision, and in my own field, robotics.

But I see several limits.

The first is data, specifically the long tail. An end-to-end model is only as good as the distribution it was trained on. Driving is mostly boring: you follow the lane, you stop at the light. The cases that actually matter for safety, like a child running out from behind a parked truck or a strange construction zone, are extremely rare. The model has to generalize to things it has barely seen. With imitation learning from human driving logs, you also inherit the fact that humans rarely demonstrate recovery from mistakes, so the model never learns what to do when it drifts off the distribution. That's the classic compounding-error problem.

The second is interpretability and verification. With a modular stack, when something goes wrong you can ask: did perception miss the object, or did the planner make a bad decision? With a pure end-to-end model, failures are much harder to attribute. For a safety-critical system that needs to be certified, explained to regulators, and debugged by engineers, that's a serious practical limit, not just a philosophical one.

The third is that "end-to-end" is never really fully end-to-end. In practice, most production systems still have auxiliary losses, intermediate representations like occupancy or lane topology, safety layers, and rule-based fallbacks. I don't think that's a failure. It's an engineering reality. The question isn't "end-to-end or not" but where you draw the learned boundary and where you keep structure.

The fourth, which I find most interesting coming from robotics, is closed-loop evaluation. Training on logged data is open-loop: the model predicts what the human did, but it never sees the consequences of its own actions. Real driving is closed-loop, and the world reacts to you. So you need good simulation, or world models, to train and test the policy in a loop. That's where I think a lot of the frontier is now: generative world models that can serve as simulators, so you can practice those rare scenarios millions of times.

So my view is that end-to-end is the right direction in the long run, because scaling learned systems has consistently beaten hand-engineering. But calling a system end-to-end doesn't solve the hard parts. The hard parts are still the long tail, closed-loop robustness, and being able to trust and verify the system. Those are where the real work is.

r001.rationale: The response defines end-to-end as mapping sensor input to actions and discusses practical system components, but does not state that models are not end-to-end because they fail to jointly integrate mapping, planning, and execution.

r002.rationale: It does not connect vehicle speed to how frequently the system must make decisions.

r003.rationale: It does not say that end-to-end models are relatively small or attribute their size to rapid decision-making.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, because "end-to-end" has become a label that papers over a lot of things.

In the strict sense, end-to-end means one network takes raw sensor input and outputs control, and the whole thing is trained with a single loss. In practice, almost nothing deployed in cars works that way. What people actually ship is a model that outputs a trajectory or a set of waypoints, and then a separate controller, often a fairly classical one, turns that into steering and throttle. Then there are safety layers, rule checks, fallback planners sitting around it. So the "end" on the output side is already not the real end.

On the input side it's similar. Many so-called end-to-end systems still have perception modules with their own supervision, like detection or occupancy heads, and the planning part reads from those intermediate representations. Gradients may flow across the boundary, but the architecture is still modular in spirit. The honest description is "differentiable pipeline," not end-to-end.

The second limit is about what the training signal can actually teach. If you're learning from human driving logs, you're doing imitation. The data is dominated by uneventful driving, and the rare, dangerous situations where you really need the model to behave well are almost absent. So you get a system that's very smooth in distribution and unpredictable out of distribution. End-to-end doesn't fix that. If anything it makes it harder to see where the failure originates, because there's no intermediate state you can point to and say, this is where the perception was wrong or this is where the planner made a bad choice.

That connects to the third thing, which is validation. With a modular stack, you can test each component against its own spec. With a monolithic model, you're mostly left with closed-loop simulation and mileage. But mileage is a weak argument for safety when the failures you care about happen once in millions of kilometers. Regulators and safety engineers want something they can decompose, and the end-to-end framing works against that.

I come from robotics and reinforcement learning, so I'll say one more thing. In robot learning, end-to-end has actually worked best when we could train in simulation with a reward, iterate a huge number of times, and then transfer. Driving has a harder version of this. The simulators are not realistic enough for the long tail, and you can't collect failure data in the real world the way you can with a quadruped falling over. So the ingredients that made end-to-end succeed in legged locomotion are only partly available here.

So my view is that end-to-end is best understood as a direction, not a destination. The useful question isn't whether a system is end-to-end but which boundaries you've removed, what you gained in capability from removing them, and what you lost in interpretability and testability. When someone uses the word as a marketing term, I'd ask them exactly that.

astra-6.text:
I think “end-to-end” is always relative to where you draw the boundaries. What is the input, and what is the output? If the input is camera images and the output is a planned trajectory, you can call that end-to-end. But there is still a controller that turns the trajectory into steering and braking, so it doesn’t mean the entire driving system is one model.

There’s also a distinction between end-to-end inference and end-to-end training. You might connect perception, prediction, and planning into one pipeline, but train them separately. Or you might have a model with internal structure and intermediate supervision, yet optimize it jointly toward the driving objective. I wouldn’t say that having intermediate representations automatically makes a system less end-to-end.

So I find the label less useful than asking what it actually buys you. Can the system learn how a perception error affects a driving decision? Can you improve the overall driving behavior rather than optimizing each component in isolation? And when something goes wrong, can you understand it and fix it reliably? End-to-end is an approach to building the system; by itself, it isn’t evidence that the system is capable or safe.

r001.rationale: The response says a controller may remain outside a trajectory-producing model, but it does not address mapping or state that mapping, planning, and execution are not jointly integrated.

r002.rationale: It does not mention high vehicle speeds or the need to make decisions at a high rate.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss model size or connect it to rapid decision-making.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “end-to-end” is always relative to the boundary you draw around a system. Where does the input begin, and where does the output stop? If a model takes camera images and produces a trajectory, you can call that end-to-end. But there is still a controller that turns the trajectory into steering and braking, and there may be safety checks around it. So it doesn’t mean the entire vehicle is one neural network.

There’s also a distinction between the architecture and how it is trained. You might connect perception, prediction, and planning in one network, but if you train each part separately, that’s different from optimizing them jointly toward the driving objective. Conversely, a system can have explicit intermediate representations and still be trained end-to-end.

So I wouldn’t treat the label itself as a measure of capability. The useful questions are: what is being optimized jointly, what assumptions are built into the system, and how do you verify its behavior when something unexpected happens? End-to-end learning can reduce the limitations imposed by hand-designed interfaces, but it doesn’t remove the need for safety engineering or validation.
